incident.title: [DEMO C037] GitHub V2 trigger setup stalls before creating a trigger
incident.description: A migrated GitHub setup job fails while creating the webhook endpoint, so no trigger instance is created despite the account being connected.

tasks.question: Scope and coordinate the evidence-led incident investigation.

What canonical trigger-worker records exist for the affected setup attempt between 2026-11-12T09:50:00Z and 2026-11-12T10:15:00Z, starting with null filters, that show the step sequence from migrated GitHub setup job start through webhook endpoint creation and any trigger-instance create call, including status, latency, retries, queue/backlog indicators, tenant/account identifiers, and exact error payloads?

Were there any changes or known degradations during the window affecting trigger-worker, the GitHub integration/auth surface, migration path logic, credential/secret access, or webhook endpoint provisioning dependencies; and do comparison records show the same setup path succeeding for other tenants/accounts in the same period?

Does the canonical evidence show the failure occurs before any request reaches GitHub or after a GitHub-facing call, and which explanation is better supported for this tenant’s failed setup: internal regression in the migrated setup path, credential/permission/configuration issue on the connected GitHub account, or provider-side failure/approval requirement?
Challenge the diagnosis, evidence grounding and verification gaps.
Write the evidence-backed internal report and proposed next steps.

objections: The evidence supports an obsolete GitHub V2 setup-path selection for the observed cedar failure, but it does not independently prove the stronger claim that a specific migrated flag or migration variant caused that path choice; keep the cause scoped to the observed V2 setup execution unless separate canonical production records identify the migration branch.

The exact 404 origin remains unverified: the record shows trigger-worker attempted /webhook_endpoints and failed before trigger creation, but does not prove whether that 404 was generated internally or by an upstream surface. That weakens boundary precision, not the observed wrong-path mechanism.

notes: Scope the single observed failure first: identify the exact setup execution/job ID, tenant/workspace, connected account, and migration flag/path used.
Use canonical source records for claims. Treat any derived connection/refresh summaries only as navigation aids, not independent proof.
Begin searches with null filters so missing timestamp/service fields do not hide relevant records; then narrow by exact-match identifiers recovered from the first pass.
Need the exact boundary where the stall happens: job accepted, webhook endpoint create attempted, endpoint persisted or not, trigger-instance create attempted or not.
Compare failure rate and latency for this path in the incident window versus nearby successful GitHub setups if available; note any backlog or queue wait that could explain a stall.
Check tenant impact explicitly: is this isolated to one tenant/account/setup execution, or are multiple tenants/setups on trigger-worker showing similar symptoms in the same window?

Distinguish mechanisms: provider failure if a GitHub call is observed and fails; permissions/config if GitHub returns an approval/authorization/resource error; internal regression if setup never reaches provider or malformed internal preconditions block endpoint creation.

Because the complaint says the account is connected, verify from canonical auth records whether the connection used by the setup was valid for the intended GitHub resource at execution time; connected does not prove adequate scope/org approval/resource access.

Look for counter-evidence: successful webhook endpoint creation followed by failure later would contradict 'stalls before creating a trigger'; a missing provider call alone is not proof without logs showing what step failed first.
Do not infer absence from partial queries. If telemetry for webhook provisioning or provider egress is missing, record that as a telemetry gap rather than concluding the action did not occur.
Useful discriminating comparison: same tenant with a non-migrated or alternate setup path, or same migrated path for another tenant/account around the same time.

Keep conclusions scoped to the observed failed execution and any directly observed affected tenants; similar historical cases or deployment timing are only hypotheses until matched by current evidence.

records.symptom: A similar workflow stopped following a release

records.summary: GitHub V2 trigger creation provisions its ingress without a separate endpoint-creation step.

notes: No trigger-worker deployment was observed in the incident window; the only deployment record is an unrelated support-dashboard release, so current evidence does not support a same-window deployment trigger for this incident.
Historical analogy about an earlier provider outage was treated as non-probative background only.

hypothesis.description: For cedar's failed GitHub V2 setup, trigger-worker appears to use an obsolete migrated setup path (/webhook_endpoints) instead of the supported V2 trigger-instance upsert path, so the failure is better supported as an internal migrated-path regression/configuration issue than as a GitHub credential, permission, or provider outage problem.
assumptions: The production log field attempted_setup_path reflects the actual path chosen by the migrated V2 setup flow.
The sandbox controlled comparison is verification only of the changed GitHub configuration/path selection, not proof of all production conditions.
The observed 404 is attributed to the internal choice of setup path; the exact upstream body is unavailable.

findings.statement: In the observed failed cedar execution, trigger-worker handled a GitHub V2 setup request with auth_valid=true but attempted setup path /webhook_endpoints and did not create a trigger, indicating failure at the setup-path stage before any successful trigger-instance creation.

A controlled sandbox comparison changed only the GitHub configuration: the original condition used /webhook_endpoints and failed 404 with no trigger created, while the corrected condition used /trigger_instances/{slug}/upsert and succeeded with trigger creation and ingress provisioning.
Public product knowledge says GitHub V2 trigger creation provisions ingress without a separate endpoint-creation step, which conflicts with the observed production attempt to call /webhook_endpoints.

Impact was material for cedar in the observed window: 370 failures out of 568 requests, 370 business operations blocked, queue depth 102, and p95 latency 1360 ms, while comparison tenant maple had 0 failures out of 494 requests, queue depth 0, and p95 latency 160 ms.
The issue is not supported as a platform-wide GitHub/provider outage because maple had a successful provider-related read in the same time slice while cedar failed.

actions: Verify the migrated GitHub V2 setup flow selects the supported trigger-instance upsert path instead of /webhook_endpoints for cedar's setup class.
Collect canonical request/response telemetry for the failed setup step, including any upstream 404 body and whether any provider egress occurred before trigger creation.
Use the controlled reproduction as a regression check for migrated GitHub V2 setup configuration/path selection.
missing_checks: Canonical provider-egress or gateway records showing whether the observed 404 was generated internally before any GitHub-facing call or returned by an upstream GitHub-facing surface.

Canonical production records tying the migrated flag/setup variant for cedar's job directly to the obsolete path selection, rather than inferring migration-path behavior from the complaint and path field alone.

hypothesis.description: A GitHub-facing or provider-surface call may have been attempted and returned 404 during cedar's setup, so an upstream/provider-side failure remains possible, but it is less supported than an internal obsolete-path problem.
assumptions: The 404 on the setup attempt could have originated from a GitHub-facing intermediary rather than purely internal validation.
The lack of provider-egress records is a telemetry gap, not proof that no upstream call occurred.

findings.statement: The canonical cedar log shows a 404 on the setup attempt, so some request stage failed before trigger creation completed.
A broad provider outage is weakened by comparison evidence: maple had a successful same-provider-related read at the same time, and the dependency snapshot reported provider API reachable.

The controlled comparison specifically shows that correcting the GitHub configuration/path resolves the failure, which argues against a generic provider outage as the primary explanation for this tenant's failed setup.

actions: Check canonical egress/gateway traces for req-37 to determine whether a GitHub-facing call actually occurred and what component returned 404.
Monitor for concurrent GitHub-facing 404s on the same setup surface before attributing this to provider instability.
missing_checks: Canonical upstream egress or response-body records for req-37 that would distinguish an internal 404 from a GitHub/provider-surface 404.

hypothesis.description: A GitHub account permission or approval issue is possible in principle for a connected account, but the supplied evidence does not specifically support organization approval, missing scope, or other account-configuration failure as the best explanation for cedar's failed setup.
assumptions: Connected accounts can still lack org approval or resource authorization, but no canonical auth or provider error payload identifying that condition is present.
auth_valid=true only indicates valid authentication, not complete authorization for every GitHub resource.

findings.statement: The failed cedar setup logged auth_valid=true, which weakens an expired or obviously invalid credential explanation for this execution.
The supplied canonical evidence has no account ID, resource target, scope list, org-approval result, or provider error body, so it cannot verify a GitHub permission/approval failure for this tenant.
The controlled reproduction resolved the failure by changing only GitHub configuration/path selection, which better fits a setup-path problem than an account-specific authorization issue.

actions: Only if path-selection evidence is disproved, inspect canonical auth/resource telemetry for the exact GitHub org/repo and whether app approval is required.
If later auth/resource telemetry specifically shows org approval blocking, request the GitHub organization owner to approve the app before retrying.
missing_checks: Canonical auth/resource-authorization records for the exact connected GitHub account and target org/repo used by cedar's failed setup.

findings.statement: The best-supported reading is that cedar's failure happened before successful trigger creation and is more consistent with an internal migrated-path/setup-path problem than with a GitHub credential or broad provider outage.
Observed impact is significant but scoped in evidence: cedar shows heavy failures and backlog, while maple remains healthy in the same window.

The supplied canonical evidence does not include provider-egress traces, upstream error body, or a production record explicitly identifying the migrated setup variant, so the exact before-vs-after-GitHub boundary is not fully proven even though the internal obsolete-path explanation is better supported.

The exact 404 origin remains unverified: the record shows trigger-worker attempted /webhook_endpoints and failed before trigger creation, but does not prove whether that 404 was generated internally or by an upstream surface. That weakens boundary precision, not the observed wrong-path mechanism.

The observed 404 is attributed to the internal choice of setup path; the exact upstream body is unavailable.

findings.statement: In the observed failed cedar execution, trigger-worker handled a GitHub V2 setup request with auth_valid=true but attempted setup path /webhook_endpoints and did not create a trigger, indicating failure at the setup-path stage before any successful trigger-instance creation.

A controlled sandbox comparison changed only the GitHub configuration: the original condition used /webhook_endpoints and failed 404 with no trigger created, while the corrected condition used /trigger_instances/{slug}/upsert and succeeded with trigger creation and ingress provisioning.
Public product knowledge says GitHub V2 trigger creation provisions ingress without a separate endpoint-creation step, which conflicts with the observed production attempt to call /webhook_endpoints.

Impact was material for cedar in the observed window: 370 failures out of 568 requests, 370 business operations blocked, queue depth 102, and p95 latency 1360 ms, while comparison tenant maple had 0 failures out of 494 requests, queue depth 0, and p95 latency 160 ms.
The issue is not supported as a platform-wide GitHub/provider outage because maple had a successful provider-related read in the same time slice while cedar failed.

actions: Verify the migrated GitHub V2 setup flow selects the supported trigger-instance upsert path instead of /webhook_endpoints for cedar's setup class.
Collect canonical request/response telemetry for the failed setup step, including any upstream 404 body and whether any provider egress occurred before trigger creation.
Use the controlled reproduction as a regression check for migrated GitHub V2 setup configuration/path selection.

hypothesis.description: A GitHub-facing or provider-surface call may have been attempted and returned 404 during cedar's setup, so an upstream/provider-side failure remains possible, but it is less supported than an internal obsolete-path problem.
assumptions: The 404 on the setup attempt could have originated from a GitHub-facing intermediary rather than purely internal validation.
The lack of provider-egress records is a telemetry gap, not proof that no upstream call occurred.

findings.statement: The canonical cedar log shows a 404 on the setup attempt, so some request stage failed before trigger creation completed.
A broad provider outage is weakened by comparison evidence: maple had a successful same-provider-related read at the same time, and the dependency snapshot reported provider API reachable.

The controlled comparison specifically shows that correcting the GitHub configuration/path resolves the failure, which argues against a generic provider outage as the primary explanation for this tenant's failed setup.

actions: Check canonical egress/gateway traces for req-37 to determine whether a GitHub-facing call actually occurred and what component returned 404.
Monitor for concurrent GitHub-facing 404s on the same setup surface before attributing this to provider instability.
missing_checks: Canonical upstream egress or response-body records for req-37 that would distinguish an internal 404 from a GitHub/provider-surface 404.

hypothesis.description: A GitHub account permission or approval issue is possible in principle for a connected account, but the supplied evidence does not specifically support organization approval, missing scope, or other account-configuration failure as the best explanation for cedar's failed setup.
assumptions: Connected accounts can still lack org approval or resource authorization, but no canonical auth or provider error payload identifying that condition is present.
auth_valid=true only indicates valid authentication, not complete authorization for every GitHub resource.

findings.statement: The failed cedar setup logged auth_valid=true, which weakens an expired or obviously invalid credential explanation for this execution.
The supplied canonical evidence has no account ID, resource target, scope list, org-approval result, or provider error body, so it cannot verify a GitHub permission/approval failure for this tenant.
The controlled reproduction resolved the failure by changing only GitHub configuration/path selection, which better fits a setup-path problem than an account-specific authorization issue.

actions: Only if path-selection evidence is disproved, inspect canonical auth/resource telemetry for the exact GitHub org/repo and whether app approval is required.
If later auth/resource telemetry specifically shows org approval blocking, request the GitHub organization owner to approve the app before retrying.

findings.statement: In the observed failed cedar execution, trigger-worker processed a GitHub V2 setup with auth_valid=true, attempted setup path /webhook_endpoints, returned 404, and did not create a trigger.

A controlled sandbox comparison changed only the GitHub configuration/path selection: the original condition used /webhook_endpoints and failed 404 with no trigger created, while the corrected condition used /trigger_instances/{slug}/upsert and succeeded with trigger creation and ingress provisioning.
Public GitHub V2 product knowledge says trigger creation provisions ingress without a separate endpoint-creation step, which conflicts with the observed production attempt to call /webhook_endpoints.

The best-supported reading is that the observed cedar failure happened before successful trigger creation and is more consistent with an internal setup-path problem than with invalid credentials or a broad provider outage.

Observed impact was material but scoped: cedar had 370 failures out of 568 requests, 370 business operations blocked, queue depth 102, and p95 latency 1360 ms, while maple had 0 failures out of 494 requests, queue depth 0, and p95 latency 160 ms.
Current evidence supports tenant-scoped impact rather than a platform-wide GitHub/provider outage because maple had a successful same-provider-related read in the same time slice while cedar failed.
A broad provider outage is further weakened by the dependency snapshot showing provider API reachable during the incident context.
The failed cedar setup logged auth_valid=true, which weakens an expired or obviously invalid credential explanation for this execution.

The supplied canonical evidence does not include provider-egress traces, upstream 404 body, retry metadata, or a production record explicitly identifying the migration branch/path-selection source, so the exact internal-versus-upstream boundary is not fully proven.

No trigger-worker deployment was observed in the incident window; the only recorded deployment was an unrelated support-dashboard release, so same-window release timing is not evidence for this trigger-worker failure.
